newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Liberals slip but still command big lead.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Liberals slip but still command big lead.

text.p: Canada's ruling Liberals have slipped marginally in the polls, partly as the result of a disastrous television performance by Prime Minister Jean Chretien, according to a new poll released on Friday.
But the Liberals maintain a commanding 30-point lead over their nearest rivals ahead of elections expected in 1997, the Angus Reid poll, commissioned for the Southam News chain, said.
The poll was conducted between Dec. 9 and 15, "in the midst of the controversy surrounding Prime Minister Chretien's position on the GST promise," Angus Reid said.

The GST is an unpopular federal goods and services tax, which contributed to the defeat of the Conservative Party government in 1993 and which Chretien promised to abolish and replace with another tax in a radio interview during the 1993 campaign.
In a "town hall" meeting broadcast on Dec. 10, a Montreal waitress asked why Chretien had not fulfilled his promise to scrap the GST.
Chretien challenged her to say on which program it was that he had promised it -- reaping the scorn of opposition parties and editorials calling him a liar.

The intensity of the political storm took time to develop, however, and would not have been covered fully throughout much of the polling period. After the polling was completed, he gave a conditional apology on the GST.

The poll showed the Liberals slipping to 46 percent from 47 percent in November and 52 percent in October. It was their lowest showing since the elections and was down from a peak of 63 percent in February 1995.
The Conservative Party slipped to 16 percent from 18 percent. The Reform Party, vying with it for the right of center, strengthened to 14 percent from 11 percent.
The leftist New Democrat Party, seen by some political analysts as a vote-drainer from the budget-slashing Liberals, were steady at 11 percent.
In Quebec, the separatist Bloc Quebecois maintained a 45-37 percent lead over the federal Liberals.
The poll surveyed 1,504 Canadian adults and would be estimated to carry a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points 19 times out of 20.
Elections are widely expected either in the spring or autumn, though they do not have to be called until late 1998.
